name: Northeastern Dinka
world_status: statement found in an open source

earlier_scan.source_named: Remijsen, Bert 2014. Evidence for three-level vowel length in Ageer Dinka (Benjamins, paywalled; abstract read — no stress statement); Blum, Mirella 2023 Suprasegmentals in three West Nilotic languages (Edinburgh thesis, ERA 403)

new_statements.quote: Described in terms of the elements distributed in it and the features which characterize it, the phonological word is the unit of stress placement in the phonological hierarchy. Each phonological word has one and only one stress. The factors that condition stress have not been studied and, as mentioned, are not the concern of this discussion. It is clear, however, that stress is neither contrastive nor used at all in connection with semantic emphasis in Dinka. The final margin of the phonological word is characterized by potential pause. The phonological word is the level of distribution of the syllable: one syllable is stressed in each word.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: QUOTE CHECK. File (102 pp., archive.org micro_IA41152914_0785, text layer present; no scanned needed). extracted text of PDF p.20 (running head 'An Overview of Dinka Phonological Structure'; the next page carries printed number 10, so PDF p.20 = printed p.9) gives sec. 2.2 'The Phonological Word' with the quoted passage word for word: 'the phonological word is the unit of stress placement in the phonological hierarchy. Each phonological word has one and only one stress. The fac-tors that condition stress have not been studied and, as mentioned, are not the concern of this discussion. It is clear, however, that stress is neither contrastive nor used at all in connection with semantic emphasi…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Dinka (all four major varieties, explicitly including Northern/Padang) has exactly one culminative stress per phonological word; the source does not say which syllable carries it ('the factors that condition stress have not been studied'), only that stress is non-contrastive and not used for emphasis. Lexical and morphological prosody is carried by tone, vowel length and voice quality (for the Ngok-Sobat variety of nort2815 see Blum 2023 ch.5: four tones L/H/HL/LH, three vowel lengths, two voice qualities). Later work on other Dinka varieties doubts a stress system altogether (Remijsen & Manyang 2009 fn.5: no acoustic support in Luanyjang; van Urk & Chong 2025: 'Dinka lacks an obvious stress system'); a 2025 instrumental investigation of Dinka stress (Blum et al. dataset) has no published result yet.
new_statements.exceptions: None; the author states that the conditioning factors have not been studied and that stress, juncture and intonation are outside the scope of the book.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the phonological word (bounded by potential pause); the examples in (5), pp. 9-10, are two-word citation phrases each carrying a single stress mark (e.g. 'mony dit 'old man', ' yok lac 'pregnant cows'), so the statement concerns word-level prominence in citation forms, not phrase-level or sentence intonation (treated separately under 2.1 with downdrift).
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted statement is pan-Dinka, not specific to Northeastern Dinka: Malou (1988: 1) says his analysis covers the four major varieties 'Eastern, which is Bor based; Northern, known as Padan, which is Donjol based; Southern which is Agar based; and Western which is Rek based', so the Northern/Padang variety (Dongjol, dong1295, a dialect of nort2815) is explicitly within scope, but the author's own variety is not stated (the sout2832 lane's internal-evidence check suggests it is neither Rek nor Agar). The same Malou passage has been recorded for sout2832 (Southwestern) and sout2834 (Southeastern); the catalog should treat it as one source claim covering all Dinka lects rather than four independent descriptions. The only first-hand descriptions of nort2815 dialects proper are tone/length studies that do not mention stress: Blum 2023 ch.5 (Ngok of the Padang cluster, speakers from the Malakal area = Ngok-Sobat ngok1245; on file) and Remijsen 2014 (Ageer agee1238; abstract only).

sources.note: Seven dialects: Abiliang abil1238, Ageer agee1238, Dongjol dong1295, Luac luac1241, Ngok-Sobat ngok1245, Rut rutt1238, Thoi thoi1238; alternative names Padang, White Nile Dinka, Nord-Dinka. Three descriptive refs (Duerksen 2004, Gilley 2004, Remijsen 2014).

sources.citation: Blum, Mirella, Maria Eduarda Goncalves Freitas, Chol Stephen Jok & Bert Remijsen. 2025. Dataset investigating syllable stress in Dinka. Harvard Dataverse. doi:10.7910/DVN/KBMYUZ
sources.note: Dataverse API record and readme: 'This dataset was collected in an investigation for the presence of syllable stress in the Dinka language. Ostensibly homophonous forms of short-stem and long-stem transitive verbs were collected to analyze whether any vocal effort measurements differ significantly'; one speaker recorded in Juba 2024; dialect not stated; the companion publication ('IsSupplementTo') is not named; no result stated.

sources.note: Agar/Luac/Bor South data (not nort2815); re-read for context: 'although Dinka lacks an obvious stress system, nothing would change if we posited abstract final stress'.

sources.citation: Blum, Mirella L. 2023. Aspects of cross-variety Dinka tonal phonology. PhD thesis, University of Edinburgh. doi:10.7488/era/3585
sources.note: Ch.5 'The tone system of Ngok Dinka' (printed pp.99-125) is a first-hand description of the Ngok dialect of the Padang cluster (three speakers, two born and raised near Malakal; sec.1.3 p.14 and fn.8), i.e. Ngok-Sobat [ngok1245] under nort2815: four tones L, H, HL, LH plus contextual tonal processes; ch.2 gives the Dinka-wide phonology (segments, syllable structure, three vowel lengths, voice quality, tone). The word 'stress' occurs only in the reference list (Gilley 2003, Hualde et al. 2002); no statement on word stress anywhere.

sources.citation: Remijsen, Bert & Caguor Adong Manyang. 2009. Luanyjang Dinka. JIPA 39(1): 113-124. doi:10.1017/S0025100308003605
sources.note: Luanyjang (Rek cluster, sout2832), not nort2815; re-read for context. fn.5 p.119: Gilley (2003) 'stress' corresponds to the morphological short grade; Remijsen & Gilley 2008 found no acoustic support for stress in Luanyjang. No placement rule.
